Surah 30: Al-Rum (The Romans)

(Meccan, except His saying ﴿So glorify God...﴾ to the end of the verse. It has sixty verses.)

﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ The discussion of it is like that which has passed concerning its counterparts among the noble opening letters.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verses 2–3:

﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ ﴿in the nearest part of the land﴾. That is: the nearest part of the land of the Arabs to them, since it is the land known to them (al-ardh al-ma'hudah 'indahum), namely the outskirts of al-Sham (Greater Syria); or, in the nearest part of their land to the Arabs. On the reading where the "al-" (the definite article in "al-ardh") is a substitute (iwad) for the genitive noun it would have replaced (al-mudaf ilayh). Mujahid said: it is the land of al-Jazirah (Upper Mesopotamia), and it is the nearest part of the land of the Romans to Persia. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: al-Urdunn and Filastin. And it was read: (adani al-ardh) ﴿and they﴾, that is, the Romans.

﴿after their defeat﴾. That is: after their being overcome. It was also read with the lam pronounced with a sukun, and this is a dialect form, like al-jalab and al-jalb.

﴿they will overcome﴾. That is: they will overcome Persia.

﴿In a few years' time﴾. It is narrated that the Persians attacked the Romans and met them at Adhri'at and Busra. It was also said that the encounter was at al-Jazira, as has already been mentioned. The Persians defeated them, and news of this reached Makkah. The polytheists rejoiced and taunted the Muslims, saying: "You and the Christians are People of the Book (ahl al-kitab, those who received earlier revealed scripture), and we and the Persians are unlettered (ummiyyun, those without scripture), and our brothers have prevailed over your brothers, so we too shall surely prevail over you." Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "May Allah not gladden your eyes! By Allah, the Romans will surely prevail over the Persians after a few years." Ubayy ibn Khalaf the accursed said to him: "You are lying. Set between us a term (ajal, a fixed period), and I will wager with you on it." So he made a wager with him for ten she-camels (qala'is) from each of them, and they fixed the term at three years. Abu Bakr informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of this, and he said: "The bid' (the phrase 'a few') is between three and nine. So increase the stake (khatar, the amount wagered)." And he extended the term, so they made it one hundred she-camels, with a term of nine years. Ubayy died from a wound inflicted by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Romans prevailed over the Persians at the beginning of the seventh year, and that was the day of al-Hudaybiyah. It was also said that victory had gone to both parties on the day of Badr, so Abu Bakr took the stake from the descendants of Ubayy and brought it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Give it in charity." This happened before the prohibition of gambling (qimar, games of chance involving wagers). These verses are among the manifest signs that testify to the truth of prophethood and to the Qur'an being from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since they reported the unseen, which none knows except the All-Knowing, the All-Aware. It has also been read as ﴿ghalabat﴾ in the active form (ghalabat, "they have prevailed"), and ﴿sa-yughlabun﴾ in the passive form (sayughlabun, "they will be overcome"). The meaning is that the Romans had prevailed over the rif al-Sham (the fertile lands of Syria), and that the Muslims would overcome them. The Muslims did indeed campaign against them in the ninth year after its revelation, and conquered some of their lands; so the attribution of the victory at that time is to the active agent.

﴿To Allah belongs the command, before and after﴾. That is: at the beginning of both periods, and at their end, when they were defeated and when they will prevail. It is as if it were said: before their being victorious, which is the time of their being defeated, and after their being defeated, which is the time of their being victorious. The meaning is that each of their being defeated first and victorious last is by nothing but the command and decree of Allah, the Exalted. ﴿And those days We alternate among the people﴾. It has also been read as ﴿min qablu wa min ba'du﴾ with a genitive (jarr) without an implied mudaf ilayhi (the noun to which the word is annexed), and with its detachment (iqtita'), as if it were said: qablan wa ba'dan, in the sense of awwalan wa akhiran (first and last).

﴿And on that day﴾, that is, the day when the Romans prevail over the Persians, and what Allah, the Exalted, had promised of their victory comes to pass.

﴿the believers will rejoice﴾.

﴿By the help of Allah﴾, and His granting victory to those who have a Book over those who have no Book, and the vexation of those among the disbelievers of Makkah who rejoiced at their (the believers') expense, and that this is one of the signs of the believers' triumph over the disbelievers. It was also said: the help of Allah is the manifestation of the truthfulness of the believers in what they had told the polytheists about the victory of the Romans over Persia. And it was said: His help, exalted is He, is that He made some of the wrongdoers rule over others and divided their word until they weakened and destroyed one another, and each of them broke the might of the other, and in that there is strength. It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, that this coincided with the Day of Badr. In it there is, for the believers, the mighty help of Allah and their joy at it, which is not hidden. The first (interpretation) is the more appropriate, because of the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿He helps whom He wills﴾, that is: whomever He wills among His servants to help against his enemy, and to make him prevail over him. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that confirms the meaning of what precedes) confirming the content of His words, exalted is He: "To Allah belongs the command, before and after" (Qur'an 30:4). ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, the one who is exceedingly possessed of might and dominance, so no one who He wills to help against him can frustrate Him, whoever that may be.

﴿The Merciful﴾, the one who is exceedingly merciful, so He helps whomever He wills to help, of whichever group it may be. And the mercy meant here is the worldly mercy. As for the well-known reading, it is clear, since neither of the two groups deserves the mercy of the Hereafter. As for the last reading, it is because the Muslims, although they deserve it, what is meant here is their help, which is among the effects of worldly mercy. And the mention of the attribute of might first is because it precedes in consideration.

ةWa'da Allah (the promise of Allah) is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing itself (mu'akkid li-nafsih), because what precedes it has the meaning of promising; it is as if it were said: "Allah promised a promise."

﴿Allah does not break His promise﴾, whatever promise it may be, of those relating to this world and the Hereafter, because lying is impossible for Him, glory be to Him. The placing of the noble Name in the position where a pronoun would be used serves to give the reason for the judgment and to magnify it. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming the meaning of the masdar, and it has been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from it, so that it is like a described verbal noun, as if it were said: "The promise of Allah is not broken."

﴿But most people do not know﴾, i.e., what has preceded of His affairs, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 7:

﴿They know an outward appearance of the worldly life﴾, which is what they witness of its adornments, its pleasures, and all its conditions that agree with their desires, suit their whims, and prompt their immersion in it and their devotion to it, not their enjoyment of its adornments and their luxuriating in its pleasures, as has been said. For these two are not among what they have come to know of it, but rather among their actions, which follow from their knowledge. The indefiniteness of "ظاهرًا" (ẓāhiran, "an outward appearance") is for belittling and disparaging, not for the sense of "one," as you may imagine; that is, they know an outward appearance of the world that is petty and base.

﴿And they are, of the Hereafter﴾, which is the ultimate goal and the most sublime aim, ﴿heedless﴾, neither bringing it to mind nor perceiving from the world what would lead to knowing it through its conditions, nor reflecting upon it, as will come. The clause is conjoined to "they know" (يَعْلَمُونَ), and its being expressed as a nominal sentence serves to indicate the continuity and perpetuity of their heedlessness. The second "hum" (هُمُ) is either an emphatic repetition of the first, or a subject (mubtada'). "Ghafilun" (غافِلُونَ) is its predicate, and the clause is a predicate of the first. On both readings, it signals the firm establishment of their heedlessness of the Hereafter, which realizes the requirement of the preceding clause, affirming their ignorance and likening them to beasts, whose perceptions of the world are confined to its base outward surfaces rather than its conditions, which are the starting points of knowledge of the affairs of the Hereafter, and indicating that the mentioned knowledge and the complete absence of knowledge are equivalent.

**Will they not reflect?** This is a rebuke and a condemnation of their narrow outlook, in confining themselves to the apparent life of this world while being heedless of the Hereafter. The *wāw* (و) here is the conjunction linking this clause to an implied clause that the context requires. God's words, **"within themselves,"** are an adverbial complement of *reflection*. Although it is clearly impossible for reflection to take place in anything other than themselves, the phrase is mentioned to confirm the matter and to depict the state of those who reflect.

God's words, **"God did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them..."** etc., are connected either to the knowledge that reflection leads to and indicates, or to the statement that follows from it, as in God's words: **"And they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: 'Our Lord, You did not create this in vain.'"** That is: have they known only the apparent life of this world, or have they confined their gaze to it, without generating reflection in their hearts, so that they would know that He, exalted is He, did not create them and what is between them of creatures, of which they themselves are a part, except in connection with some purpose?

**"Except with truth"**: or that they would say this statement while acknowledging its content after knowing it. By **"truth"** is meant that which is established and which must necessarily be established, because it is founded upon profound wisdom and a sound purpose, namely that created beings serve as evidence for accountable people, through their essences, attributes, and changing states, of the existence of their Creator, exalted and mighty is He, of His oneness, His knowledge, His power, His wisdom, His exclusive right to worship, and the veracity of His reports, among which is their being brought back to life after annihilation to eternal life, and their being recompensed according to their deeds, once the good is distinguished from the wicked, and the ranks of the individuals of each of the two groups are differentiated according to the differentiation of the levels of their knowledge and beliefs, which are determined by their outlooks. This is in what has been placed in created things of signs, proofs, indications, and tokens, as His words express: **"And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed."** Indeed, *deed* (ʿamal) is not restricted to the deeds of the limbs, and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it by saying: **"Which of you is best in intellect, most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of God, and quickest in obedience to God."** Its verification has already passed at the beginning of Surah Hud, peace be upon him.

God's words, **"and a specified term,"** are a conjunction linked to *truth*. That is: and with a specified term that God, exalted is He, has decreed for their continuance, by which they must inevitably end, and that is the time of the Hour.

Furthermore, it has been permitted that God's words **"within themselves"** be a complement of *reflection* in the sense: "Have they not reflected within themselves, which are the creatures nearest to them, and they know their affairs best and are more informed of their states than of the states of anything else, so that they would contemplate what God, exalted is He, has deposited in them, outwardly and inwardly, of marvelous wisdoms that indicate providential management and not neglect?" And that they must come to an end at a time when the Wise One who arranged their affairs will recompense them: good for good, and for evil its like, so that at that time they would know that the affairs of all other creatures likewise proceed according to wisdom and providence, and that they must come to that time. You are aware that the affair of human resurrection and recompense for what they did of evil and good is the matter intended in itself, and the one most in need of proof. Therefore, making it a means to prove the resurrection of others, while it is far removed from recompense, is an inversion of the matter. So reflect.

God's words, **"Indeed, many of the people are, in the meeting with their Lord, disbelievers,"** are a concluding statement that confirms what precedes it, by clarifying that most of them are not limited to the heedlessness about the conditions of the Hereafter that was mentioned, and to their turning away from reflecting on what would guide them to knowing it, from the creation of the heavens and the earth and the created things between them. Rather, they deny and reject the meeting with His reckoning and His recompense through resurrection.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 9:

﴿Have they not travelled in the land?﴾ This is a rebuke to them for not taking warning from witnessing the conditions of their like, which point to their final outcome and destination. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for affirming what is negated, and the waw is for coordination (ʿatf) upon an implied element required by the context, meaning: "Have they sat in their places? Have they not travelled ﴿in the land﴾?" The saying of the Exalted, ﴿so that they might see﴾, is coordinated upon "travelled" and falls under the ruling of affirmation and rebuke. The meaning is that they have travelled through the regions of the earth and witnessed ﴿how was the end of those before them﴾ from the destroyed nations, such as ʿAd and Thamud. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿they were greater than them in strength﴾ ... etc., is an explanation of the beginning of their conditions and their outcome; that is, they were more capable than these people of enjoying the life of this world, since they were stronger than them.

﴿And they tilled the earth﴾, that is, they turned it over for cultivation and sowing. It has been said: for extracting water, extracting minerals, and other things.

﴿And they built it up﴾, that is, those people built it up with various kinds of cultivation, planting, construction, and other things that count as building it up.

﴿More than these have built it up﴾, that is, a building up greater in quantity, quality, and duration than the building up of these people of it. How could it not be so? For they were people of a valley without cultivation, with no expansion for them elsewhere. In this there is mockery of them, since they were deceived by the world and proud of its goods despite the weakness of their state and the narrowness of their resources, for the matter of worldly affairs depends on expansion in the lands, dominion over the servants, and moving about in the sides of the earth with all kinds of activities, while they were weak people compelled to a valley with no benefit in it, fearing that people would snatch them away.

﴿And their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, that is, with miracles or clear signs.

﴿So God would not have wronged them﴾, that is, they denied their messengers, so He destroyed them; God would not have destroyed them without a sin on their part requiring it. The expression of this as "wronging," although God's destroying them without sin is not wronging at all according to the established principle of the People of the Sunna, is to show the perfection of His exaltedness above that by presenting it in the form of what cannot proceed from Him, the Exalted. It has passed in Surah al-Anfal and Surah Al ʿImran.

﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾, by daring to commit what necessitates it of great sins.

[Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 15:]

﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, delighted.﴾ This is a detailed explanation of the conditions of those two groups. The *rawḍah* (meadow) is every land having vegetation, water, splendour, and freshness. It is indefinite for the sake of magnification, and what is meant by it is Paradise. *Al-ḥubūr* is joy. It is said: *ḥabarahu* when it gave him joy such that his face beamed. It is also said: *al-ḥabarah* is every fine blessing, and *al-taḥbīr* is beautification. From Ibn Kaysan: they will be adorned with jewelry (*yuḥallawna*). From Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash: crowns upon their heads. From Waki': music in Paradise.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): he mentioned Paradise and the blessings in it. At the rear of the people was a Bedouin who said: "O Messenger of Allah, is there any music in Paradise?" He (ﷺ) said: "O Bedouin, indeed in Paradise there is a river whose two banks are virgins, from every fair-skinned one of the *khawṣāniyyah* type, who sing with voices such as creation has never heard before.
