Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 16:

﴿And as for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs﴾ which include these signs that articulate what has been detailed.

﴿And the meeting of the Hereafter﴾ He stated this explicitly, although it is included in the denial of the signs, out of concern for its matter. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then those﴾ is a reference to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in view of its being characterized by what is within the scope of the relative clause (al-silah) of disbelief and denial of His signs, exalted is He, and of the meeting of the Hereafter. This is to announce the complete distinction of them by that from others, and their being aligned in the row of those who are witnessed. And what is in it of the meaning of distance, despite the recency of the reference, is to indicate the remoteness of their rank in evil, i.e., those described by what has been detailed of abominations.

﴿Will be brought forth into the punishment﴾ perpetually, never to be absent from it.

﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ ﴿and to Him belongs all praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you enter the noon﴾. After He had explained the condition of the two groups, the believers who do righteous deeds and the disbelievers who deny Our signs, and what reward and punishment each of them has, they were commanded with that which saves from the second and leads to the first: glorifying Allah, exalted is He, by declaring Him free of everything unfitting to His majesty, glorified is He, and praising Him, exalted is He, for His great blessings. The first (glorification) is placed before the second (praise) because clearing (takhliyah, removing defects) precedes adornment (tahliyah, adorning with virtues). The "fa" (al-fa', the particle of consequence) indicates that what follows it results from what precedes it, meaning: when you know this, then glorify Allah, exalted is He, that is, declare Him free of what He, glorified is He, has been described with, that is, glorify Him in the manner fitting to these times. And praise Him, for the report that praise belongs to Him, exalted is He, and that it is obligatory for the discerning among the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, carries in meaning a command to praise Him in the most emphatic and forceful manner. Placing praise between the times of glorification serves to give it importance and to indicate that the two should be combined, as His words, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿And we glorify You with Your praise﴾ and His words, exalted is He: ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord﴾. And the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever says, when he enters the morning and when he enters the evening, 'Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him,' one hundred times, his sins are removed even if they were like the foam of the sea." And his words (ﷺ): "Whoever says, when he enters the morning and when he enters the evening, 'Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him' one hundred times, no one will come on the Day of Resurrection with anything better than what he brought, except one who said the same as he said or more." And his words (ﷺ): "Two words, light on the tongue, heavy in the scale: Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him, Glory be to Allah the Mighty." Besides these, there are countless other verses and hadiths. The specifying of these two (glorification and praise) to those times is to indicate that what occurs in them of the signs of His power, and the effects of His mercy and His blessing, are clear witnesses to His transcendence, exalted is He, and His deserving of praise, and necessarily require His glorification and praise without doubt. His words, exalted is He: ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾ are coordinated with ﴿when you enter the evening﴾, and its placement before ﴿and when you enter the noon﴾ is for the sake of observing the verse-endings (fawasil, the rhyming pauses of the verses). The change of expression (from "when you enter" to "and in the late afternoon") is because the verb is not derived from it in the sense of entering a period of 'ashi (late afternoon), as with al-masa' (evening), al-sabah (morning) and al-zuhayrah (noon). Perhaps the secret in this is that 'ashi is not one of the times in which people's conditions vary, and change noticeably, so as to justify describing them as leaving what precedes it and entering what follows it, as with the mentioned times. For each of those is a time in which conditions change visibly. As for evening and morning, this is evident. As for noon, it is a time in which people customarily strip off their garments for the midday rest, as was mentioned in Surat al-Nur. It has been said that what is meant by glorification and praise is the prayer, since it includes both. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the verse comprises the five daily prayers: "when you enter the evening" refers to the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers, "when you enter the morning" refers to the Fajr prayer, "in the late afternoon" refers to the 'Asr prayer, and "when you enter the noon" refers to the Zuhr prayer. For this reason al-Hasan held that it is Medinan, since he used to say that the obligatory (prayer) in Mecca was two rak'ahs at whatever time they coincided, and that the five were only prescribed in Medina. The majority hold that they were prescribed in Mecca, and this is the correct view, because of the hadith of the Night Journey (al-Mi'raj, the Ascension), at the end of which is: "They are five prayers each day and night." From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever would like to be measured out for with the full measure (qafiz al-awfa, a large measuring vessel), let him say: 'So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning'" ... to the end of the verse. And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever says, when he enters the morning: 'So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning,' up to His words, exalted is He: 'And thus you will be brought forth,' he will attain what he missed in his day. And whoever says it when he enters the evening, will attain what he missed in his night." It has also been read: (ḥīnan tumsūna wa-ḥīnan tuṣbiḥūna), meaning: you enter (the evening) at it and you enter (the morning) at it.

﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ ﴿and to Him belongs all praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you enter the noon﴾. After He had explained the condition of the two groups, the believers who do righteous deeds and the disbelievers who deny Our signs, and what reward and punishment each of them has, they were commanded with that which saves from the second and leads to the first: glorifying Allah, exalted is He, by declaring Him free of everything unfitting to His majesty, glorified is He, and praising Him, exalted is He, for His great blessings. The first (glorification) is placed before the second (praise) because clearing (takhliyah, removing defects) precedes adornment (tahliyah, adorning with virtues). The "fa" (al-fa', the particle of consequence) indicates that what follows it results from what precedes it, meaning: when you know this, then glorify Allah, exalted is He, that is, declare Him free of what He, glorified is He, has been described with, that is, glorify Him in the manner fitting to these times. And praise Him, for the report that praise belongs to Him, exalted is He, and that it is obligatory for the discerning among the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, carries in meaning a command to praise Him in the most emphatic and forceful manner. Placing praise between the times of glorification serves to give it importance and to indicate that the two should be combined, as His words, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿And we glorify You with Your praise﴾ and His words, exalted is He: ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord﴾. And the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever says, when he enters the morning and when he enters the evening, 'Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him,' one hundred times, his sins are removed even if they were like the foam of the sea." And his words (ﷺ): "Whoever says, when he enters the morning and when he enters the evening, 'Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him' one hundred times, no one will come on the Day of Resurrection with anything better than what he brought, except one who said the same as he said or more." And his words (ﷺ): "Two words, light on the tongue, heavy in the scale: Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him, Glory be to Allah the Mighty." Besides these, there are countless other verses and hadiths. The specifying of these two (glorification and praise) to those times is to indicate that what occurs in them of the signs of His power, and the effects of His mercy and His blessing, are clear witnesses to His transcendence, exalted is He, and His deserving of praise, and necessarily require His glorification and praise without doubt. His words, exalted is He: ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾ are coordinated with ﴿when you enter the evening﴾, and its placement before ﴿and when you enter the noon﴾ is for the sake of observing the verse-endings (fawasil, the rhyming pauses of the verses). The change of expression (from "when you enter" to "and in the late afternoon") is because the verb is not derived from it in the sense of entering a period of 'ashi (late afternoon), as with al-masa' (evening), al-sabah (morning) and al-zuhayrah (noon). Perhaps the secret in this is that 'ashi is not one of the times in which people's conditions vary, and change noticeably, so as to justify describing them as leaving what precedes it and entering what follows it, as with the mentioned times. For each of those is a time in which conditions change visibly. As for evening and morning, this is evident. As for noon, it is a time in which people customarily strip off their garments for the midday rest, as was mentioned in Surat al-Nur. It has been said that what is meant by glorification and praise is the prayer, since it includes both. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the verse comprises the five daily prayers: "when you enter the evening" refers to the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers, "when you enter the morning" refers to the Fajr prayer, "in the late afternoon" refers to the 'Asr prayer, and "when you enter the noon" refers to the Zuhr prayer. For this reason al-Hasan held that it is Medinan, since he used to say that the obligatory (prayer) in Mecca was two rak'ahs at whatever time they coincided, and that the five were only prescribed in Medina. The majority hold that they were prescribed in Mecca, and this is the correct view, because of the hadith of the Night Journey (al-Mi'raj, the Ascension), at the end of which is: "They are five prayers each day and night." From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever would like to be measured out for with the full measure (qafiz al-awfa, a large measuring vessel), let him say: 'So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning'" ... to the end of the verse. And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever says, when he enters the morning: 'So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning,' up to His words, exalted is He: 'And thus you will be brought forth,' he will attain what he missed in his day. And whoever says it when he enters the evening, will attain what he missed in his night." It has also been read: (ḥīnan tumsūna wa-ḥīnan tuṣbiḥūna), meaning: you enter (the evening) at it and you enter (the morning) at it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 19:

﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾, like a human from a drop (nutfah), and a bird from an egg.

﴿And He brings forth the dead from the living﴾: the drop and the egg from the animal.

﴿And He revives the earth﴾ with vegetation ﴿after its death﴾, its drying up.

﴿And thus﴾, and similar to that bringing forth, ﴿you will be brought forth﴾ from your graves. It has also been read as (takhrujun), with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the ra', and this is a kind of elaboration of His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Allah originates creation, then repeats it﴾.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 20:**

﴿And among His signs﴾ (are the manifest ones that clearly indicate that you will be resurrected, a clearer indication than what came before). The indication of the initial creation of them is more evident for their recreation than the indication of bringing the living out of the dead, bringing the dead out of the living, and the indication of the earth's revival after its death.

﴿That He created you﴾, i.e., within the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, because it has been stated repeatedly that his (ﷺ) creation encompasses the creation of his descendants in a summary manner.

﴿from dust﴾, which never smelled the scent of life, and there is no correspondence between it and what you are in your essence and attributes.

﴿Then, behold, you are human beings spreading out﴾, i.e., after that you suddenly became human beings dispersing through the earth. This is the summary of what was detailed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O people, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed, We created you from dust, then from a drop of semen...﴾ ... to the end of the verse.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 21:**

﴿And among His signs﴾, which indicate what was mentioned of resurrection and what follows it of recompense.

﴿That He created for you﴾, i.e., (p-56) for your sake.

﴿From yourselves, mates﴾. The creation of the origin of your spouses, Hawwa' (Eve), from the rib (ḍil‘) of Adam, peace be upon him, implies their creation from yourselves, according to the verification you have learned, or [it means] from your own kind and not from another kind. The latter is more suitable to His words, exalted is He: ﴿That you may find rest in them﴾, i.e., that you may become attached to them, incline toward them, and be at peace with them. Indeed, sameness of kind is one of the causes of closeness and mutual acquaintance, just as difference is one of the causes of separation and aversion.

﴿And He placed between you﴾, i.e., between the spouses. This is either by *taghlīb* (the rhetorical device of giving precedence to men over women in address), or by omitting an adverbial phrase coordinated with the one mentioned, meaning: He placed between you and them, as has passed in His words, exalted is He: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾. It has also been said: or between the individuals of the kind, i.e., between men and women. But His words, exalted is He, ﴿affection and mercy﴾, rule this out, for what is meant by them is definitely what exists between them by the bond of marriage. That is, He placed between you, through the marriage He prescribed for you, affection and compassion, without there being between you any prior acquaintance or any tie of kinship or blood relation that would justify mutual sympathy. It has been said: "affection and mercy" come from God, exalted is He, while *al-fark* (the harshness/quarrelling) comes from Satan. It is related from al-Hasan, may God have mercy on him, that "affection" is a metaphor for intercourse and "mercy" a metaphor for offspring, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and mercy from Us﴾.

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, i.e., in what was mentioned of their creation from dust, the creation of their spouses from themselves, and the placing of affection and mercy between them, and the demonstrative's sense of distance together with the recentness of the reference, is to indicate the elevated rank of what is pointed to.

﴿Are signs﴾, great ones, whose true nature cannot be fully comprehended, numerous, whose measure cannot be estimated.

﴿For a people who reflect﴾ upon the interstices of those firm acts founded on consummate wisdom. The sentence is a concluding clause (*tadhyīl*) confirming the content of what precedes it, together with an alert that what was mentioned is not a single sign, as His words, exalted is He, ﴿And among His signs﴾ indicate, but rather it comprises various signs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 22:

﴿And among His signs﴾ — indicating what has been mentioned concerning the matter of the Resurrection and what follows it of recompense.

﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ — either in that the One Who is able to create them, with what is in them of created things, without a prepared matter for them, is more evidently capable of restoring what was alive before that; or in that their creation and what is in them is only for the livelihood of mankind and its return (to Him). This is made clear by His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is in the earth﴾ [2:29], and His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He might test you [as to] which of you is best in deed﴾ [11:7].

﴿And the diversity of your tongues﴾ — that is, your languages: in that He taught each kind its language, inspired it with its formation, and enabled it to use it; or [it refers to] the kinds of your speech and its forms, for you hardly hear two speakers who are equal in manner in every respect.

﴿And the diversity of your colors﴾ — by the whiteness of the skin, its blackness, and its being between the two; or by the formations of the limbs, their shapes and their colors and their features, such that distinction between individuals is achieved by them, to the extent that twins, despite the agreement of their matter and their causes and the circumstances that converge upon them in their formation, differ in some of that without doubt, even if they are in the utmost resemblance. This has been placed in the thread of the cosmic signs, the creation of the heavens and the earth, although it is among the inner signs, truly deserving of being arranged in the thread of what preceded concerning the creation of their own selves and their spouses, to announce its independence and to guard against the supposition that it is among the complements of their creation.

﴿Indeed in that﴾ — that is, in what has been mentioned of the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the diversity of tongues and colors — ﴿are signs﴾ — great in themselves, abundant in number.

﴿For those who know﴾ — that is, those characterized by knowledge, as in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And none understands them except those who have knowledge﴾ [29:43]. It has been read with the letter lam vowelled with a fatha, and in this is an indication of the complete clarity of the signs and that they are not hidden from any of creation whatsoever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 23:

﴿And among His signs is your sleep by night and by day﴾ for the rest of the psychic faculties (al-quwa al-nafsaniyya), and the strengthening of the natural faculties (al-quwa al-tabi'iyya).

﴿and your seeking of His bounty﴾ in both of them. For each of sleep and the seeking of bounty occurs in both of the two periods (al-malawayn), although the more common pattern is the occurrence of the first in the first and the second in the second, or: your sleep by night and your seeking by day, as is customary, and in accordance with the other verses that address this matter. Except that He separated the first two correlates by the last two correlates, because they are a time (zaman). And time together with what occurs within it is like one thing, with the arrangement of the wording (al-laff) aiding unity.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who hear﴾ meaning: it is their condition to hear speech with the hearing of understanding (tafahhum) and insight (istibsar), wherein they reflect upon the nuances of this exposition and draw inferences from it concerning His exalted affairs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 24:

﴿And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning﴾. The verb (fi'l) here is either implicitly governed by "an" (that), as in the words of the one who said:

"O you who rebuke me, bring me to the battle (al-waghā)"

That is: "an uḥḍir" (that I should attend).

Or it is treated as occupying the place of a verbal noun (maṣdar), and in this sense is explained the well-known proverb, "You hear of al-Mu'aydi (a man of the Mu'aydi, an unknown figure) and it is better than that you see him." Or it stays as it is and functions as an attribute (ṣifah) of an omitted noun, meaning: "a sign by which He shows you the lightning," like the words of the one who said:

"And time is nothing but two alternations (tārratān), of which one is death, and in the other I seek life and strive."

That is: "of them, at one time I die in it, and at another I seek in it." Or the meaning is: "and among His signs is something, or a cloud, which shows you the lightning."

﴿Fear﴾ of the thunderbolt, or for the traveller.

﴿And hope﴾ for the rain, or for the one who stays at home. Their being in the accusative is as a reason (ʿillah) for a verb implied by what was mentioned, for showing them the lightning necessarily entails their seeing it. Or they are a reason for the mentioned thing itself, with an omitted modifier such as "the showing of fear and hope." Or, by interpreting fear and hope as causing fear and causing hope, as in your saying: "I did it in spite of (raghman) Satan." Or they are in the accusative of state (ḥāl), as in "I spoke to him face to face (shifāhan)."

﴿And He sends down from the sky water﴾, and it is read with the light form (takhfīf). ﴿Then He gives life thereby to the earth﴾ with vegetation.

﴿After its death﴾, its dryness.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who use reason﴾, for they are so manifest that mere reason suffices to perceive them when it is employed in deducing their causes and the manner of their formation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 25:

﴿And of His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command.﴾ That is, by His, may He be exalted, will for their standing. Expressing this by "command" indicates the perfection of power and independence from means and causes. The meaning of their being established is not their creation, since that has already been clarified by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. Nor is it their standing without an observable supporter, as has been said. That is among the completions of their creation, even though it is not stated explicitly, relying on what was mentioned in more than one place in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He created the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾ ... the verse. (p-58) Rather, it is their standing and continuance in their present state until their appointed term, which His saying, may He be exalted, earlier expressed: ﴿Allah created the heavens and the earth and what is between them only with truth and for a specified term﴾. Since this verse comes after the rest of the enumerated signs, and is connected to the resurrection in existence, it was placed after them and was also connected to it in mention. Thus it was said: ﴿Then when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you emerge﴾. For this is a statement directed toward informing of the occurrence of the resurrection, and its existence after the end of the term of their standing is a consequence of enumerating the signs that indicate it, not included in their series, as has been said. It is as if it were said: "And of His signs is the standing of the heavens and the earth in their forms, by His command, may He be exalted, until a specified term which He, may He be exalted, determined for their standing. Then when He calls you," that is, after the expiry of the term, "from the earth," while you are in your graves, "with one call," by saying: "O dead, come out," you will suddenly come out from them. That is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On that day they will follow the caller﴾. And "from the earth" is related to ﴿He calls you﴾, since it suffices for that that the one called is in it. It is said: "I called him from the bottom of the valley, so he came up to me," and not related to ﴿you emerge﴾, because what follows ﴿idhā﴾ (إذا, "when/then") does not govern what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 26:

﴿And to Him belongs﴾ exclusively ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ of the angels, and of the two weighty ones (mankind and jinn), in creation, dominion, and disposal, with no partner to Him in that in any way whatsoever.

﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾, i.e., they are submissive to His action and do not resist Him in any of His affairs, exalted is He.

﴿And He it is who originates creation, then repeats it﴾ after their death. Its repetition serves to strengthen the affirmation and to prepare for what follows it, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾, that is, in relation to your measure. The reasoning is by analogy (qiyas) to your own principles, since otherwise both are equal for Him. It has been said that "أهون" (ahwan, "easier") means "هيّن" (hayyin, "easy"). The pronoun is masculine though it refers back to the repetition (al-i'ada), because the repetition is interpreted as "that He repeats." It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the creation (al-khalq), but this is not the right view. As for what is said, that origination (al-insha') by way of bounty, in which the agent has the choice between doing and not doing, and that repetition is of the category of the obligatory, which must necessarily be done, so that it is closer to occurrence than origination, which is uncertain between occurrence and non-occurrence and thus far from attainment, this is not correct. The intended sense of the act being "easier" is not that it is closer to existence in terms of the number of factors prompting the agent to bring it about and the strength of their demand for the connection of His power to it. Rather, it means the ease of its being accomplished and its issuing from Him after His power has been connected to its existence, and its being necessitated by another. There is no difference in this between that connection occurring by way of necessity or by way of choice.

﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness﴾, that is, the supreme attribute, wondrous in its nature, of all-encompassing power, perfect wisdom, and all other attributes of perfection, none of which anyone else can approach, let alone equal. As for the one who interpreted it as the statement "There is no god but Allah," he intended by it the attribute of oneness (al-wahdaniyya).

﴿in the heavens and the earth﴾ is connected to the meaning of the preceding clause, in the sense that He has been described by it and made known in them through the tongues of creatures and through the tongues of the signs. It has also been said that it is connected to "the highest," and it has been said that it is connected to a omitted element, which is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from Him, or from "the likeness," or from its pronoun in "the highest."

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, the one who is capable and is not unable to originate what is possible, or to repeat it. ﴿the Wise﴾, the one who conducts actions according to the courses of wisdom and benefit.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 28:

﴿He has propounded for you a parable from yourselves.﴾ By it the invalidity of association (shirk) is made manifest.

﴿From yourselves﴾ means: drawn from their own states, which are the nearest matters to you, the most familiar to you, and the most evident in indicating what was mentioned of the invalidity of shirk, because they are by way of priority (bi-tariq al-awlawiyya). And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do you have﴾ ... etc., is a depiction of the parable, i.e., "Do you have?"

﴿From what your right hands possess﴾, of slaves and maidservants, ﴿as partners in what We have provided you﴾ of wealth and what goes in its course, of that over which you exercise disposal. So the first "min" (in min ma malakat) is for the starting point (ibtida'iyya), the second is partitive (tab'idiyya), and the third is superfluous (mazida), for emphasizing the negation derived from the interrogative. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so that you are equal therein﴾ is a confirmation of the meaning of partnership and an explanation that they and their partners are equal in disposing of what was mentioned, without any preference for them over it. This is on the basis that there is an omitted element conjoined to "antum" (you), not that it is general to both parties by way of predominance (taghlib). That is: Are you content for yourselves? While your slaves are like you in humanity and its rulings, that they should share with you in what We have provided you, and it is lent to you, so you and they are equal therein, disposing of it as you dispose, without any difference between you and them.

﴿You fear them﴾ is another predicate of "antum" (you), or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the agent in "sawa'" (equal), i.e., you apprehend that you would act independently in disposing of it without their opinion.

﴿As you fear each other, your own selves﴾ means: a fear similar to your fear of the free persons who share with you in what was mentioned. The meaning is the negation of the content of what the interrogative sentence detailed, i.e., you are not content that your slaves, who are like you in humanity and are not created for you but for God exalted, should share with you in what is lent to you. How then do you associate with Him, glorified is He, in worship, which is among His essential attributes, a created being, indeed a product of His creation, since you make it with your own hands and then worship it?! ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that clear detailing.

﴿We detail the signs﴾, i.e., We make them clear and explain them, not with any detailing less than this, for the parable is a depiction of intelligible meanings in the form of the perceptible, and a bringing forth of the wild perceptions in the form of the familiar, so it is in the utmost clarity and explanation.

﴿For a people who reason﴾, i.e., who employ their intellects in reflecting upon matters. Their being singled out for mention, despite the generality of the detailing of the signs to all, is because they are the ones who benefit from them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 29:

﴿Rather, those who did wrong follow their desires﴾ is a turning away from addressing them and an attempt to guide them to the truth through setting forth examples, detailing the signs, and employing sound, rational premises, and it is an explanation of the impossibility of their following the truth. It is as if it were said: they did not understand anything of the detailed signs, but rather they followed ﴿their desires﴾, the deviant ones. Placing the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in the place of their pronoun serves to record against them that in that following they are ﴿those who did wrong﴾, placing things in other than their proper place, or wronging themselves by exposing themselves to the everlasting punishment.

﴿Without knowledge﴾, that is: ignorant of the falsehood of what they adopted, devoted to it, with no deterrent turning them away from it, unlike the knowing person who, when he follows falsehood while knowing its falsehood, is turned away from it.

﴿So who can guide one whom Allah has led astray﴾, that is: whom Allah has created misguidance in by directing his choice toward his own acquisition; that is, no one is able to guide him.

﴿And they have no﴾, that is: for the one whom Allah the Exalted has led astray, and the plural is used in view of the meaning.

﴿helpers﴾ who would rescue them from misguidance and protect them from its consequences and afflictions, in a sense that none of them has a single helper, according to the rule of matching plural with plural.

(p-60) ﴿So set your face toward the religion⁠﴾ is a figurative expression for turning towards the religion, being upright in it, steadfast upon it, and being concerned with arranging its means. For whoever is concerned with a thing perceptible by sight fixes his gaze upon it, directs his look at it, and straightens his face toward it, facing it. That is: so straighten your face toward it, and make it upright, not turning right or left. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿upright (ḥanīfan)⁠﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring either to the one commanded or to the religion.

﴿The fiṭrah of Allah⁠﴾: al-fiṭrah means the innate disposition (al-khalqah). Its being in the accusative is by way of incitement (al-igrā'), meaning: adhere to it; or it means: [adhere to] the fiṭrah of Allah upon you, since the address is to everyone, as His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿turning back in repentance (munībīna)⁠﴾ makes clear. The singular in "set (aqim)" is because the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the imam of the community, so his command implies their command. To adhere to it means to proceed in accordance with its requirements and not to neglect it by following desire and the enticement of the devils. It has also been said that it is in the sense of the verbal noun, meaning: Allah originated a fiṭrah (faṭara Allāhu fiṭratan). His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿upon which He created mankind⁠﴾ is a qualifier of "fiṭrat Allah," emphasizing the obligation to comply with the command, since Allah's creation of people upon His fiṭrah, which is an expression for their acceptance of the truth and their capacity to perceive it, or for the religion of Islam, is among the requirements for adhering to it and holding fast to it with certainty. For if they were left alone with what they were created upon, it would lead them to it, and they would not choose any other religion over it. Whoever among them goes astray does so through the misguidance of the devils of mankind and jinn. From this is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, relating from the Lord of Might: "Every one of My servants was created upright (ḥunafā'), then the devils led them astray from their religion and commanded them to associate others with Me." And his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "Every child is born upon the fiṭrah, until his parents make him a Jew or a Christian." His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿There is no alteration to the creation of Allah⁠﴾ is a justification for the command to adhere to the fiṭrah of Allah, Exalted is He, or for the obligation to comply with it. That is: there is no validity or rectitude in altering it by neglecting its requirement and not carrying out its demand by following desire and accepting the whisperings of the Satan. It has also been said: no one is able to change it. Then, in that case, the alteration must be understood as altering the fiṭrah itself by removing it entirely and placing another fiṭrah in its stead, one that is not sound for accepting the truth and being able to perceive it. This is because the alteration in the first sense is within capacity, indeed it certainly occurs. The justification then is that the soundness of the fiṭrah is realized in every person, so it is necessary to adhere to it by acting upon its requirements, and not to neglect this by what has been mentioned of following desire and the steps of the Satan.

﴿That⁠﴾ refers to the religion commanded to be the object of setting the face toward it, or to adherence to the fiṭrah of Allah derived from the incitement, or to the fiṭrah if it is interpreted as the religion. The masculine form is due to the interpretation of the thing mentioned, or in consideration of the predicate.

﴿The upright religion⁠﴾: the straight, even one in which there is no crookedness.

﴿But most people do not know⁠﴾ this, so they turn away from it with aversion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 31:

﴿Turning back to Him﴾ is a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier) from the pronoun in the implied verb that governs "the nature of God" (﴿fitrata Allah﴾), or from the imperative "establish" (﴿aqim﴾), given its generality to the community, as has been indicated. What lies between them is an *i'tiraḍ* (parenthetical clause). That is: returning to Him, from *anaba*, which means to return repeatedly, one time after another, as opposed to *raja'a*, which means to return once. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and fear Him﴾, means: from opposing His command. It is a conjunction (*'atf*) upon the implied verb mentioned. Likewise His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and establish the prayer, and do not be among the polytheists﴾, those who alter the nature of God, exalted is He, with an alteration.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 32:

﴿Of those who have split up their religion⁠﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the polytheists," with the preposition repeated. Their splitting up of their religion is their disagreement concerning what they worship, according to the divergence of their desires (p-61). The benefit of this substitution (ibdal) is to warn against aligning oneself with a faction (hizb) among the factions of the polytheists, by making clear that all of them are upon manifest misguidance. It has also been read as (faraqu) — meaning they abandoned their religion which they had been commanded to follow.

﴿And they became sects⁠﴾ — that is, groups (firaq), each of which follows the leader (imam) who misled it.

﴿Every faction, rejoicing in what they have⁠﴾ — of the crooked religion founded upon corrupt opinion and false claim.

﴿Rejoicing⁠﴾ — pleased, thinking it to be the truth, and how could it be so? Thus the sentence is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) confirming the content of what precedes it, namely their splitting up of their religion and their becoming sects. It has also been permitted that "rejoicing" be an attribute (sifah) of "every," with the predicate being the fronted adverbial phrase, namely "of those who split up," but its remoteness is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 33:

﴿And when harm touches mankind﴾, i.e., hardship (shiddah).

﴿they call upon their Lord, turning back in repentance to Him﴾, returning to Him from calling upon anyone else.

﴿Then when He lets them taste mercy from Him﴾, deliverance from that hardship.

﴿Behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord﴾, the One whom they had called upon, turning to Him in repentance.

﴿ASSOCIATE OTHERS﴾ (yushrikun): i.e., a group of them suddenly commit shirk (ishrak, associating partners with God). The restriction of this action to some of them is because some of them are not like that, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when He brings them safely to land, some of them are moderate (muqtasid)﴾, i.e., remaining upon the middle path (al-tariq al-qasd), or moderate (mutawassit) in disbelief, since he is restrained to some extent.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 34:

﴿So that they may disbelieve in what We have given them.﴾ The lam here is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah, indicating the outcome), and it has been said that it is the lam of a threatening command (lam al-amr al-tahdidi). It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So enjoy yourselves, but soon you will know.﴾ However, the shift (iltifat, a change in grammatical person) here is for emphasis (mubalaghah). It has been read as (wa-liyatamatta'u, "and let them enjoy themselves") ﴿but soon you will know﴾ the outcome of your enjoyment. It has also been read with the ya' (yā’, third-person prefix), on the basis that tamatta'u is a past tense verb, and the shift to the third person (al-iltifat ila al-ghaybah) is in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Or have We sent down to them⁠﴾ to signal turning away from them, and to enumerate their crimes against others in a direct manner (bruntly, *mubaththah*).

﴿Authority⁠﴾ means a clear proof. It has also been said: "possessing authority," meaning a dominion accompanied by a proof.

﴿So it speaks⁠﴾ speaks in the sense of indication, as in His words, ﴿This Our Book speaks against you with truth⁠﴾, or speaks in the sense of articulate speech.

﴿Of what they used to associate with Him⁠﴾: with their associating (partners) with Him, Exalted is He, or with the matter because of which they associate (partners).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 36:

﴿And when We let the people taste mercy﴾ i.e., a blessing of health and abundance.

﴿they rejoice in it﴾ out of insolence and exultation, not out of praise and gratitude.

﴿And if an evil befalls them﴾ i.e., hardship, ﴿because of what their hands have sent forward﴾ because of the ill consequences of their sins, ﴿behold, they despair﴾ they suddenly fall into despair of God's mercy, exalted is He. It is also read with a kasra on the nun (yaqnitun).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 37:

﴿Do they not see﴾ that is: Do they not look and not witness?

﴿That Allah extends provision to whomever He wills and restricts it﴾. Then why do they not give thanks, and why do they not seek reward in times of ease and hardship as the believers do?

﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾, so that they may infer from them the perfection of power and wisdom. (p-62)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 38:

﴿So give to the near of kin his right﴾, from the (ṣilah) kinship ties, and charity (ṣadaqah), and all other acts of goodness (mabarrāt).

﴿And the needy and the wayfarer﴾, [give them] what they deserve. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, or to whoever has been given abundance, as the particle "fa" (so) indicates.

﴿That is best for those who desire the Face of Allah﴾, meaning His essence (dhāt), or His direction (jihah). By "their charity" they intend Him, the Exalted, sincerely, or the direction of drawing near to Him and not any other direction.

﴿And those are the ones who are successful﴾, in that by what was given to them they attained everlasting bliss (al-ni'īm al-muqīm).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 39:

﴿And whatever you give as riba﴾ is an increase that carries no equivalent exchange in the transaction. It is also read as (ātaytum) with a short vowel (qasr), meaning: you fell into it or were overtaken by it, through giving riba.

﴿That it may increase within the wealth of people﴾ — that it may grow and multiply in their wealth.

﴿It does not increase with Allah﴾ — i.e., it is not blessed. It is also read as (li-tarbū), meaning: so that you may increase, or so that you may become people of riba.

﴿And whatever you give in zakat, seeking the Face of Allah﴾ — i.e., seeking by it His exalted Face, sincerely.

﴿Those are the ones who receive multiplied reward﴾ — i.e., possessors of multiplied (adʿāf) reward from the reward. The counterpart of al-mud'if (the one who multiplies) is al-muqwi (the one who is strong) and al-mūsir (the one who is wealthy, possessing ease), for one who has strength and ease; or it means those who have multiplied their reward and their wealth through blessing. It is also read with a fatḥah on the ʿayn. The change in the noble composition and the shift (iltifāt) contain a grandeur that is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 40:

﴿It is Allah who created you, then provided for you, then will cause you to die, then will bring you to life. Is there any of your partners who does anything of that?﴾ He, exalted is He, affirmed for Himself the necessary attributes of divinity (al-uluhiyyah) and its distinctive properties, and He negated them outright from what they took as partners to Him, exalted is He, from idols and others, emphasizing the denial regarding what proof (burhan) and direct observation (ʿiyan) establish, and on which there is consensus (wifaq). Then He drew a conclusion from it, namely His transcendence above partners, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate.﴾

It has been permitted that the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) be a qualifier (sifah), with the predicate (khabar) being "is there any of your partners," and the connecting element (al-rabit) being His saying, exalted is He, "of that," since it carries the meaning of "of its actions" (min af'alihi). The first "min" and the second "min" indicate the generality (shuyu') of the ruling over the class of partners and actions, while the third "min" is additional (mazidah) to generalize the negated element, and each of them independently serves for emphasis. It is also read: (tushrikun) in the second-person form of address.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 41:

﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea﴾ such as drought, dead lands, frequent burning, drowning, the failure of seafaring voyages, the loss of blessings, the abundance of harms, or misguidance and injustice. It has been said: the meaning of "the sea" is the settlements of the coasts and the settlements of the seas.

﴿Because of what the hands of people have earned﴾ due to the ill omen of their sins, or by their earning them. It has been said: corruption appeared on land by the killing of Qabil (Cain) of his brother Habil (Abel), and at sea by the fact that Jalanda (p-63) used to seize every ship by force.

﴿That He may let them taste some of what they have done﴾ i.e., some of its recompense, for its full completion is in the Hereafter. The "lam" (la) here indicates cause (ta'lil), or consequence (al-'aqibah). It is also read as (linudhiqahum) with the nun, ﴿so that they may return﴾ from what they were upon.

Say, "Travel through the earth and see what was the end of those before you." So that they may witness their remains.

"Most of them were polytheists." This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) indicating that what befell them was due to the widespread prevalence of polytheism among them; or, polytheism was prevalent among most of them, while the sins other than it were found among only a few of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 43:

﴿So set your face toward the upright religion﴾. That is: the one perfect in uprightness (al-baligh al-istiqamah).

﴿Before there comes a Day which none can turn back﴾. No one is able to turn it back.

﴿From Allah﴾. This is connected either to "yati" (comes) or to "maradd" (turning back), since it is a verbal noun (masdar). The meaning is that Allah Most High does not turn it back, because His eternal will is tied to its coming.

﴿On that Day they will be divided﴾. Its original form is "yatasadda'un", meaning they will separate: a group in the Garden and a group in the Blazing Fire (al-sa'ir).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 44:

﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief.﴾ That is: its burden (wabal) is upon him, and it is the everlasting Fire.

﴿And whoever does righteousness, for themselves they prepare [a resting place].﴾ That is: they make ready (yusawwuna) a dwelling place in Paradise. The fronting of the prepositional phrase (zarf) in both places serves to indicate exclusivity (ikhtisas).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 45:

﴿So that He may reward those who believe and do righteous deeds out of His bounty.﴾ It is connected to "yusadda'un" (they will be divided), and it has been said that it is connected to "yamhadun" (they prepare the way for themselves), meaning: they will be separated, by Allah the Exalted dividing them into two groups, so that He may reward each of them according to their deeds. Since the reward of the believers was the primary intended outcome, He highlighted it in the context of the purpose (ghaya), and expressed it by the term "bounty" (fadl), because reward given by way of grace (tafaddul) is not obligatory (wujub). The reward of the other group is alluded to by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers.﴾ For the absence of His love, the Exalted, is a metonymy (kinaya) for His hatred, which necessarily entails His wrath, which in turn necessarily entails punishment.

And among His signs is that He sends the winds, namely the north wind, the east wind (al-Saba), and the south wind (al-Janub). For these are winds of mercy. As for al-Dabur (the west wind), it is a wind of punishment. From this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "O Allah, make them winds, and do not make them a wind." It has also been read as "al-rih" (the wind) with the intention of the genus.

﴿Bearing good news﴾ of rain, ﴿and that He may let you taste of His mercy﴾, which is the benefits that follow from them. It has been said that it means the fertility that follows the descent of rain caused by them, or the comfort that comes with their blowing. The "lam" (the particle of purpose, al-lam) is connected to "yursil" (He sends). The clause is coordinated with "mubashshirat" (bearing good news) in meaning, as if it were said: "so that He may give you good news by them, and so that He may let you taste." Or it is connected to an elided element understood from the mention of the sending, its estimated form being: "and so that He may let you taste, and so that it may be such-and-such; He sends them for no other purpose unrelated to your benefits."

﴿And that the ships may sail﴾ by His command, ﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ through the trade of the sea, ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾, and that you may thank Allah's favour for what has been mentioned of the sublime ends. (p-64)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 47:

﴿And We certainly sent before you messengers to their peoples﴾ just as We sent you to your people.

﴿And they brought them clear proofs﴾ That is: every messenger came to his people with the clear proofs specific to him, just as you came to your people with your own clear proofs. The "fa" (فَ) in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So We took vengeance upon those who committed crime﴾ is a fa' fasiha (فَاءٌ فَصِيحَةٌ, an "eloquent fa" that signals an omitted clause), meaning: they denied them, so We took vengeance upon them. He placed the relative pronoun "them" (ضَمِيرَهُمُ المَوْصُولَ) rather than a simple pronoun in order to draw attention to the place of what was omitted, and to indicate that it is the cause of the vengeance. In His words, exalted is He, ﴿And it was incumbent upon Us to help the believers﴾ there is an additional honouring and dignifying of the believers, in that they are made deserving, with respect to Allah exalted is He, of His helping them, and an indication that the vengeance against the disbelievers was for their sake. It is possible to pause at "ḥaqqan" (حَقًّا) with it being connected to the vengeance. Perhaps the placing of this noble verse in the manner of a parenthetical interjection (اعْتِراض, i'tira±) between what preceded and what followed concerning the conditions and rulings of the winds is to warn the disbelievers and caution them against neglecting the obligations of the required gratitude, by His words, exalted is He, ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾, in return for the countable blessings tied to sending them, lest there befall them a like calamity that befell those peoples, of vengeance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 48:

﴿Allah is He who sends the winds﴾ — a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought to explain what was left general (ujmila) earlier concerning the states of the winds.

﴿So they stir up clouds, and He spreads them﴾ — spreading them out in the sky, sometimes connected (muttasilan) ﴿in the sky﴾, that is, in its atmosphere (jawwiha).

﴿as He wills﴾ — moving along and standing still, spread out completely (mutbaqan), not spread out completely but open on one side and not on another, and other than that.

﴿And He makes them fragments (kisafan)﴾ at another time, that is, pieces (qit'an). It has been read with a sukun on the sin, which would then be a lightened plural of (kisfah), or a verbal noun (masdar) described by it.

﴿Then you see the rain (al-wadq)﴾ — the rain.

﴿coming out from within it﴾ — in both states.

﴿Then when He causes it to fall upon whomever of His servants He wills﴾ — that is, upon their lands and their territories.

﴿Behold, they rejoice﴾ — they suddenly (fuja'u) rejoice at the coming of fertility (al-khisb).

﴿وَإنْ كانُوا﴾ "in" (إنْ) is the lightened form of "inna" (إنَّ), and its subject, the pronoun of the matter (ضَمِيرُ الشَّأْنِ, ḍamīr al-sha'n, the dummy pronoun), is omitted. That is, "and indeed the matter was that they were."

﴿مِن قَبْلِ أنْ يُنَزَّلَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ That is, the rain.

﴿مِن قَبْلِهِ﴾ This repetition is for emphasis, and to signal how long they had been without rain and how firmly their despair from it had set in. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the rain, or to the clouds, or to the sending down. It has also been said that it refers to the "kisf" (the dimming or eclipse of the sun or the sky), on the recitation with a sukun (quiescent pronunciation, qirā'a bi-l-sukūn). This is not clear. Closer to the point is that the pronoun refers to the "istibshār" (joyful expectation). The phrase "min" is connected to "yunazzilu" in order to convey the swiftness with which their hearts turn from despair to joyful expectation, by indicating how close together the two times are, through showing that despair is linked to the sending down, which is in turn linked to joyful expectation, as attested by the sudden "idhā" (إذا الفُجائِيَّةُ, idhā al-fujā'iyya, the "idhā" of sudden occurrence).

﴿لَمُبْلِسِينَ﴾ This is the predicate (خَبَرُ, khabar) of "kānū." The "lām" (اللّامُ, al-lām) is the lām that distinguishes the predicate from the negative (اللّامُ الفارِقَةُ, al-lām al-fāriqa, the distinguishing lām), that is, that they are indeed despairing. Meaning: "in despair."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 50:

﴿So look at the effects of Allah's mercy﴾, which are consequent upon the sending down of rain, (producing) plants, trees, and various kinds of fruits. The "fa" (fa, "so") indicates the swiftness of their consequence upon it. It is also read (athar) in the singular (tawhid). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿how He gives life﴾, i.e., Allah, exalted is He, ﴿to the earth after its death﴾, is in the place of the accusative by removal of the preposition. "Kayfa" (kayfa, "how") is an interrogative clause suspending the verb "look" (nazara), meaning: so look at His wondrous giving of life to the earth after its death. It is said that it is in the adverbial position (al-hal) by interpretation. Whatever the case, the purpose of the command to look is to draw attention to the immensity of His power, exalted is He, and the vastness of His mercy, together with what it paves the way for regarding the matter of resurrection that follows it. It is also read (tuhyi) in the feminine, on the basis of attribution to the pronoun of mercy.

﴿Indeed, that﴾, the One of great affairs, some of whose affairs have been mentioned, ﴿is the Giver of life to the dead﴾, i.e., He is capable of giving them life, for it is a bringing into being of the like of what was in the substance of their bodies of the animal powers, just as the giving of life to the earth is a bringing into being of the like of what was in it of the vegetative powers. Or (it means) that He will certainly give them life. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and He is over all things Powerful﴾, is a concluding statement affirming the content of what precedes it, i.e., He is absolutely powerful over all things, of which their giving of life is one, since the relation of His power to all of them is equal.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 51:

﴿And if We sent a wind, and they saw it﴾ — that is, the effect indicated by the effects (athar), or the vegetation expressed by the word "effects" (al-athar), for it is a noun of genus (ism jins) that encompasses the little and the much.

﴿yellowed﴾ after its greenness. It has been permitted that the pronoun refers to the clouds, since if it were yellowed it would not rain; but its remoteness is not hidden. The lam in ﴿la-in﴾ is a preparatory lam (lam al-muwatta'ah) for the oath, entering upon the conditional particle. The fa' in ﴿fa-ra'awhu﴾ is a fa' of elucidation (fa' fasihah). The lam in His words, exalted is He, ﴿la-zallu﴾ is the lam of the answer to the oath, standing in place of both answers. That is: by Allah, if We send a wind, hot or cold, and it strikes their crop so that it becomes yellow, and they see it yellowed, they will surely remain...

﴿after it, they disbelieve﴾ without hesitation. In this is a censure of them, after their steadfastness, and of the speed of their wavering between the two extremes of excess and deficiency, which is not hidden, since it was obligatory upon them to rely upon Allah, exalted is He, in every state, to turn to Him with seeking forgiveness when the rain is withheld from them, not to despair of the mercy of Allah, exalted is He, to hasten to thankfulness through obedience when He afflicts them with His mercy, not to be excessive in rejoicing, and to be patient under His trial when a blight afflicts their crop, and not to disbelieve in His blessings. But they reversed the matter, refused what would benefit them, and committed what would ruin them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 52:

﴿So indeed you cannot make the dead hear﴾ because they are like them, since their faculties are closed off from the truth.

﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn their backs and flee﴾ The restriction of the ruling to what has been mentioned serves to explain the full extent of the wretched state of the disbelievers, and to alert that they combine two evil traits: the deafness of their ears to the truth, and their turning away from listening to it. Had only one of them been present in them, that would have sufficed for them; so how much more so now that they have combined both. For the deaf person who faces the speaker may perceive, from his postures and gestures, something of his speech even though he does not hear it at all. But when he turns away from it, he hardly understands anything from it at all. And it was read: with a fatha on the ya' (تُسْمِعُ read as yusma'u, with the subject being the deaf), and with the ṣumm in the nominative (رَفْعِ الصُّمِّ).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 53:

﴿Nor canst thou guide the blind out of their error.﴾ They are called "blind" either because they have lost the true purpose of sight, or because of the blindness of their hearts. It is also read: "tahdi al-'umy" (you guide the blind).

﴿You cannot make to hear﴾, i.e., you cannot make to hear anything.

﴿Except those who believe in Our signs﴾, for their faith calls them to reflect upon them and to receive them with acceptance; or, except those who are close to believing in them and turn to them with a fitting turning.

﴿So they are Muslims﴾, submitting to what you command them of the truth.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 54:

(p-66) ﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾. (Allah) is the subject and the predicate, i.e., He originated you as weak ones, and made weakness the foundation of your affair, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And man was created weak﴾, i.e., He created you from a weak origin, which is the drop (nutfah).

﴿Then He made after weakness strength﴾. That is at your reaching puberty (ihtilam), or at the attachment of the soul (ruh) to your bodies.

﴿Then He made after strength weakness and gray hair﴾, when old age takes hold of you. It has also been read with a ḍammah on the ḍād throughout, and that is stronger, due to the saying of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both: "I recited it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he recited it to me as min ḍu'f." Both are dialectal variants, like al-faqr and al-fuqr. The indefiniteness together with the repetition is because the first (weakness) is not the same as the latter.

﴿He creates what He wills﴾ of things, of which what has been mentioned of weakness, strength and gray hair is part.

﴿And He is the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful﴾, the one who is exceeding in knowledge and power, for the alternation through these varied stages is among the clearest proofs of knowledge and power.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 55:

﴿And on the day the Hour [al-sa'ah] is established﴾ — that is, the Resurrection (al-qiyamah), so called because it is established (taqumu) at the last hour (akhir sa'ah) of the hours of this world; or because it comes suddenly (baghtatan), and it has become its distinctive name, like the star (al-najm) for the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), and the planet (al-kawkab) for Venus (al-Zuhrah).

﴿The criminals will swear that they had not remained﴾ — that is, in the graves, or in the world. The first is the more apparent, because their remaining is delimited by the Day of Resurrection (yawm al-ba'th), as will come. Their remaining in the world is not thus delimited. It has been said: [it is] the period between the passing away of the world and the Resurrection, and the cessation of their punishment. And in a hadith: "What is between the passing away of the world and the Resurrection is forty," and this admits of hours, days, or years. It has also been said: it is not known whether it is forty years or forty thousand years. ﴿Except an hour﴾ — they considered the duration of their remaining to be little, through forgetfulness, or lying, or guesswork.

﴿Thus they used to be turned away﴾ — in the manner of that turning away, they used to be turned away in the world from the truth and sincerity.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 56:

﴿And those who were given knowledge and faith said﴾, in the world, [namely] among the angels and humankind.

﴿"You have indeed remained within the Book of God"﴾, that is, in His knowledge, or in His decree, or in what He has written and determined, or in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh), or the Qur'an. And this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And behind them is a barzakh (barrier)"﴾ [23:100].

﴿"until the Day of Resurrection"﴾. By this they refuted what they had said, and they confirmed it with an oath. As if, from the extremity of their bewilderment, they did not realize that this was the promised Resurrection which they had been denying, and which they used to hear would take place after the annihilation of all creation, and they used to reckon for it a lengthy span of time, even though they did not believe in its realization. So the people of knowledge rejected their statement and alerted them to the fact that they had remained until a distant term which they used to hear of and deny. They rebuked them by informing them of its occurrence, when they said: ﴿"So this is the Day of Resurrection, but you used to deny it"﴾, the one you were promised in the world.

﴿"But you did not know"﴾ that it is true, so that you would hasten toward it in mockery. The "fa'" (fa) here is the answer to an elided conditional clause, as in the words of the one who said:

Verse: They said, "Khurasan is the farthest that is aimed at us, then the return; indeed we have come to Khurasan."

Verse 57: ﴿So on that Day, their excuse will not benefit those who did wrong﴾ — that is, their excuse (ʿudhr). It is also read "tanfaʿu" with the feminine ta', observing the apparent wording of the expression, even though a separator intervenes between them. (p-67)

﴿Nor will they be asked to make amends﴾ — they will not be called to that which would bring about their being pleased (iʿtāb), that is, the removal of their displeasure (ʿatb) through repentance and obedience, as they were called to it in the world. From their saying: "Fulān asta'tabanī, fa-aʿtabtuhu," meaning: he asked me to be pleased, so I pleased him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 58:

﴿And indeed We have set forth for mankind in this Qur'an every kind of example.﴾ That is: by Allah, We have indeed made clear to them every condition, and described for them every attribute, such that it is, in its strangeness, like an example; and We have related to them every story of wondrous matter, such as the description of those raised up on the Day of Resurrection, their story, what they say, what is said to them, and what is done to them, including the rejection of their excuses.

﴿And if you bring them a sign﴾ from the signs of the Qur'an that speak of such things,

﴿those who disbelieved will surely say﴾ out of excessive their obstinacy, stubbornness, and hardness of heart, addressing the Prophet ﷺ and the believers:

﴿"You are nothing but falsifiers."﴾ That is: you are nothing but fabricators (mubtilun, i.e., those who produce falsehood and invent lies).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 59:

﴿Thus﴾ like that vile sealing.

﴿Thus Allah seals the hearts of those who do not know﴾ they do not seek knowledge, nor do they seek out the truth; rather they persist in superstitions they have come to believe and in baseless nonsense which they have invented. For compound ignorance (al-jahl al-murakkab, the state of not knowing that one does not know) prevents the perception of truth and necessitates the denial of the one who speaks the truth.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 30, verse 60:**

﴿So be patient﴾ in the face of what we witness from them of false statements and evil deeds. ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾. He has promised you victory, the manifestation of the religion, and the elevation of the word of truth, and it must be fulfilled and carried out without doubt.

﴿And let them not disquiet you﴾: let them not drive you to haste and agitation.

﴿Those who have no certainty﴾ regarding what you recite to them of the clear signs, by denying them and by harming you with their falsehoods, among which is their saying: "You are nothing but men of falsehood." Indeed, they are doubters and misguided, and such things are not improbable from them. It has also been read with a light nun (وَلا يَسْتَخِفَّنَّكَ, pronounced with the nun lightened), and it has been read as ﴿وَلا يَسْتَحِقَّنَّكَ﴾ from the (علم) istihqaq (claiming a right), meaning: let them not tempt you so that they possess you and become more entitled to you than the believers. Whatever the case, the apparent sense of the noble wording, although it is a prohibition addressed to the disbelievers against belittling him (ﷺ) and claiming a right over him, is in reality a prohibition addressed to him (ﷺ) against being affected by their belittling and being tempted by their temptation, by way of metonymy (kinaya), as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And let not the hatred of a people prevent you from acting justly﴾.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Rum will have ten good deeds recorded for him for each angel that glorifies Allah the Exalted between heaven and earth, and he will make up for what he missed during his day and night."
